meaning: Asks how someone feels about something, how things are going, or what they think. It is also used to offer or suggest something.
connection: Noun + は + どうですか／いかがですか

senses.label: Asking for impressions
senses.meaning: Asks how the listener feels about something, or how it's going: “How is ...?” For past experiences, use 「どうでしたか」.
senses.connection: Noun + はどうですか／はどうでしたか (often with 仕事, 生活, 味, 天気, etc.)
examples: How is life in Japan?
How was yesterday's test?
How does it taste?

senses.label: Offering something
senses.meaning: Offers food, drinks or things: “Would you like ...?” Use the more polite 「いかがですか」 with guests and older people.
senses.connection: Noun + はいかがですか／はどうですか (often with お茶, コーヒー, お菓子, etc.)
examples: Would you like some coffee?
How about some of this cake, too?

senses.label: Suggesting a time or plan
senses.meaning: Suggests a time, place or plan and asks if it works: “How about ...?” 「いかがでしょうか」 is the very polite version.
senses.connection: Time / place noun + はどうですか／はいかがでしょうか
examples: How about tomorrow afternoon?
Would next Monday work for you?

notes: 「いかが」 is the polite form of 「どう」. 「いかがですか」 sounds better with guests, bosses and older people.
Between friends, shorten it to 「〜はどう？」 or 「〜、どう？」.
To accept an offer, say 「ええ、いただきます」. To decline, say 「いいえ、けっこうです」.
「〜たらどうですか」 with a verb gives advice. It is a different pattern.

daily.title: Asking a friend how things are
daily.description: Your friend just started a new job, and you ask how it's going.
daily.example: How's the new job?

daily.title: A guest at home
daily.description: The host serves tea and snacks to a visiting friend.
daily.example: Would you like some tea?

daily.title: Making plans with a friend
daily.description: Deciding on a day to meet up.
daily.example: How about Saturday?

work.title: Setting a time with a client
work.description: Suggesting a visit time to a client with the formal 「いかがでしょうか」.
work.example: Would ten o'clock next Wednesday work for you?

work.title: A waiter's suggestion
work.description: A waiter offers something to a customer.
work.example: Would you like dessert after your meal?

etymology: 「どう」 is a question word asking about manner or state: “how”. 「いかが」 is thought to come from old 「いかにか」 (如何にか) through sound changes. It is more refined and polite than 「どう」. It can be written 「如何」, but kana is normal.

similar.title: 〜たらどうですか
similar.explanation: 「〜たらどうですか」 follows a verb and gives advice: “Why don't you ...?” 「〜はどうですか」 follows a noun and asks for impressions or offers something.

similar.title: 〜どんな
similar.explanation: 「どんな + noun」 asks about kind or nature: “what kind of ...?”, as in 「どんな人ですか」. 「〜はどうですか」 asks for an opinion or impression.

similar.title: 〜ませんか
similar.explanation: 「〜ませんか」 uses a verb to invite someone to do something together, as in 「一緒に行きませんか」. 「〜はどうですか」 offers or suggests a noun (a thing or a time).

title: 〜に〜回 (frequency)
meaning: Says how many times something is done within a period of time: “... times a day / a week”.
connection: Time-period noun + に + number + 回／度

senses.label: ... times per ...
senses.meaning: Tells how many times something happens in a unit of time. The period goes before 「に」; the number of times goes before 「回」.
senses.connection: 一日・一週間・一か月・一年, etc. + に + number + 回
examples: I take medicine three times a day.
I swim in the pool twice a week.
I watch a movie once a month.

senses.label: Asking how often
senses.meaning: Use 「何回」 to ask how often: “How many times a ...?” Answer with the same pattern.
senses.connection: Time-period noun + に + 何回 + 〜ますか
examples: How many times a week do you play sports?
How many times a day do you brush your teeth?

senses.label: Once in a long while
senses.meaning: 「〜に一度」 also shows frequency. When 「十年に一度」 or 「百年に一度」 describes a noun, it means something very rare.
senses.connection: Time-period noun + に + 一度 (+ の + noun)
examples: I go back to my country once a year.
This is the heaviest snow in ten years.

notes: In speech and on labels, 「に」 is often dropped, as in 「一日三回」 on a medicine bag.
Both 「回」 and 「度」 count times. 「度」 is a bit more formal and is mostly used with small numbers like 「一度」 and 「二度」.
Don't put 「に」 after 「毎日」 or 「毎週」: 「毎日二回」, not ✕「毎日に二回」.
「三回目」 means “the third time” (order), not frequency.

daily.title: Getting medicine
daily.description: A pharmacist tells a patient how often to take the medicine.
daily.example: Please take this medicine twice a day, morning and night.

daily.title: Talking about hobbies
daily.description: Telling a friend how often you go to the gym.
daily.example: I go to the gym three times a week.

daily.title: Going home
daily.description: An international student says how often they go back home.
daily.example: I go back to my country once a year.

work.title: Explaining the meeting schedule
work.description: Telling a new coworker how often regular meetings are held.
work.example: We have meetings twice a month.

work.title: Equipment checks
work.description: The person in charge explains how often a machine is inspected.
work.example: We inspect this machine once every six months.

etymology: Here 「に」 marks the unit for a rate, like “per”. 「回」 originally meant “to turn, go around once”, and came to mean “times”. 「度」 originally meant “measure, scale”, and also came to mean “times”.

similar.title: 〜目 (ordinal)
similar.explanation: 「三回目」 means “the third time”, which is order. 「週に三回」 means “three times a week”, which is frequency.

similar.title: 〜おきに
similar.explanation: 「一日おきに」 means “every other day” and focuses on the gap. 「一日に一回」 is the number of times per unit of time.

similar.title: 〜ずつ
similar.explanation: 「一人に二つずつ」 means giving an equal share to each person. 「〜に〜回」 only means times per unit of time.

meaning: Says that two things are the same: “the same as ...”.

senses.label: Same as (predicate)
senses.meaning: Comes at the end of the sentence and says A and B are the same. The negative is 「〜と同じではない」 or 「〜と違う」.
senses.connection: AはBと同じだ／同じです
examples: My birthday is the same day as my mother's.
These shoes are the same as my old ones.

senses.label: The same ... as (before a noun)
senses.meaning: Describes the noun after it: “the same ... as ...”. 「同じ」 goes straight before a noun, with no 「な」.
senses.connection: Bと同じ + noun (クラス・会社・色, etc.)
examples: I go to the same school as my older brother.
Do you have a pen in the same color as this one?

senses.label: In the same way as
senses.meaning: 「〜と同じように」 describes a verb: “do it the same way as ...”.
senses.connection: Bと同じように + verb
examples: Please pronounce it the same way the teacher does.

senses.label: A and B are the same
senses.meaning: List the two things with 「と」, then say 「は同じだ」: “A and B are the same.”
senses.connection: AとBは同じだ／AもBも同じだ
examples: My older sister and I are in the same class.
These two kanji have the same meaning.

notes: Don't add 「な」 before a noun: ✕「同じな色」, ○「同じ色」.
But before 「の」, 「ので」 and 「のに」, use 「同じな」: 「同じなのに」, 「同じなので」.
For the same degree, use 「〜と同じくらい」: 「父と同じくらい背が高い」 (as tall as my father).

daily.title: Ordering at a restaurant
daily.description: You see what your friend ordered and want the same.
daily.example: I'll have the same as him, please.

daily.title: A coincidence
daily.description: Chatting with a new friend, you find out you share a birthday.
daily.example: Oh, we have the same birthday!

daily.title: Looking for something in a shop
daily.description: Holding an old item, you ask the clerk for the same kind.
daily.example: Do you have the same battery as this one?

work.title: Explaining steps
work.description: A senior coworker asks a new employee to follow a sample.
work.example: Please make it the same way as this sample.

work.title: Checking a document format
work.description: Confirming that a new document uses the same format as last time.
work.example: The same format as last time is fine.

etymology: 「同じ」 comes from an old adjective 「同じ（おなじ）」. It is a special word that goes straight before a noun without 「な」. The 「と」 marks what is being compared.

similar.title: 〜と (and / with)
similar.explanation: 「と」 alone means “and” or “with”. In 「〜と同じ」, 「と」 marks what you compare with: “the same as ...”.

similar.title: 〜ような・〜みたいな
similar.explanation: 「〜のような」 means “like ...”. It is a comparison or an example, and the two are not exactly the same. 「〜と同じ」 means they really are the same.

similar.title: 〜と違う
similar.explanation: The opposite: “different from ...”. 「AはBと違う」 is close to 「AはBと同じではない」.

meaning: Pronouns that point to things: “this”, “that”, “that (over there)” and “which”, chosen by distance from the speaker and the listener.
connection: Used alone, as subject, object, etc. (これは／それを／どれが, etc.)

senses.label: これ: this
senses.meaning: Points to a thing near the speaker: “this (one)”. It can stand alone as subject or object.
senses.connection: これ + は／が／を, etc.
examples: This is my book.
I'll take this one, please.

senses.label: それ: that (near you)
senses.meaning: Points to a thing near the listener. It also refers to what the other person just said: “that”.
senses.connection: それ + は／が／を, etc.
examples: What is that?
A: Tomorrow is a day off. B: That's nice.

senses.label: あれ: that (over there)
senses.meaning: Points to a thing far from both speaker and listener. It also refers to a past event both people remember: “that”.
senses.connection: あれ + は／が／を, etc.
examples: That's the station over there.
That was a fun trip, wasn't it?

senses.label: どれ: which
senses.meaning: A question word: “which one?” among three or more things. As a subject, use 「が」, not 「は」.
senses.connection: どれ + が／を／です, etc.
examples: Which one is your umbrella?
Which one will you have?

notes: 「これ・それ・あれ・どれ」 are pronouns and can't go right before a noun: ✕「これ本」, ○「この本」.
Use 「が」 after 「どれ」 as a subject: ○「どれが安いですか」, ✕「どれは安いですか」.
When choosing between two things, use 「どちら／どっち」, not 「どれ」.
To refer to something just mentioned, use 「それ」. Use 「あれ」 for something both people remember.

daily.title: Shopping
daily.description: A customer points at an item in the case and speaks to the clerk.
daily.example: Excuse me, could you show me that one?

daily.title: Asking about a place
daily.description: Pointing at a building in the distance and asking a friend.
daily.example: What's that building over there?

daily.title: Choosing a present
daily.description: A friend shows you a few things to choose from.
daily.example: Which one do you think is good?

work.title: Handing over documents
work.description: Explaining as you give a coworker some papers.
work.example: These are the materials for tomorrow's meeting.

work.title: Checking files
work.description: Your boss asks which of the papers on the desk is the final version.
work.example: Which one is the latest version?

etymology: Japanese demonstratives come in sets called “ko-so-a-do”: 「こ」 is near the speaker, 「そ」 near the listener, 「あ」 far from both, and 「ど」 is the question form. 「〜れ」 is the ending for things. The same system includes 「ここ」 (places) and 「この」 (before nouns).

similar.title: 〜この・その・あの・どの
similar.explanation: 「この・その・あの・どの」 must be followed by a noun (この本). 「これ・それ・あれ・どれ」 stand alone (これは本です).

similar.title: 〜ここ・そこ・あそこ・どこ
similar.explanation: The 「ここ」 set points to places; the 「これ」 set points to things.

similar.title: 〜こんな・そんな・あんな・どんな
similar.explanation: The 「こんな」 set means “this kind of / that kind of”. It is about kind or nature and comes before a noun.

title: 〜この・その・あの・どの + noun
meaning: Words placed before a noun to show which one is meant: “this ...”, “that ...”, “that ... (over there)”, “which ...”.
connection: この／その／あの／どの + noun

senses.label: この: this ...
senses.meaning: Describes something near the speaker: “this ...”. It must be followed by a noun.
senses.connection: この + noun
examples: This book is interesting.
How much is this bag?

senses.label: その: that ... (near you)
senses.meaning: Describes something near the listener, or something just mentioned: “that ...”.
senses.connection: その + noun
examples: Is that umbrella yours?
I met a friend yesterday. That person is a doctor.

senses.label: あの: that ... (over there)
senses.meaning: Describes something far from both people, or a person or thing both people know: “that ...”.
senses.connection: あの + noun
examples: Who is that person over there?
The ramen at that shop was good, wasn't it?

senses.label: どの: which ...
senses.meaning: A question word: “which ...?” among three or more. It is followed by a noun.
senses.connection: どの + noun + が／を, etc.
examples: Which train will you take?
Which color do you like?

notes: 「この・その・あの・どの」 can't stand alone: ✕「このはペンです」, ○「これはペンです」.
In speech, 「あの」 or 「あのう」 is also a filler like “um...” when you start talking. This is different from pointing.
「どの」 is for three or more choices. For two, use 「どちらの」.

daily.title: At a clothing store
daily.description: A customer points at a shirt near the clerk.
daily.example: Could you show me that shirt?

daily.title: Asking at the station
daily.description: Asking staff which bus to take.
daily.example: Which bus should I take to Shinjuku?

daily.title: Remembering the past
daily.description: Talking with a friend about a place you went to together.
daily.example: That park brings back memories, doesn't it?

work.title: Checking a document
work.description: Pointing at the papers in your hand and confirming with a coworker.
work.example: Please send these materials by the end of today.

work.title: Booking a meeting room
work.description: Asking a coworker which meeting room is free.
work.example: Which meeting room is free?

etymology: Made from a ko-so-a-do prefix plus 「の」, which links to a noun: 「こ＋の」, 「そ＋の」, 「あ＋の」, 「ど＋の」. That's why they only come before a noun and describe it.

similar.title: 〜これ・それ・あれ・どれ
similar.explanation: The 「これ」 set are pronouns and stand alone. The 「この」 set must take a noun. 「これは本です」 vs. 「この本は…」.

similar.title: 〜こんな・そんな・あんな・どんな
similar.explanation: 「この本」 means this specific book. 「こんな本」 means “this kind of book”, focusing on its nature or type.

similar.title: 〜の (possession / describing)
similar.explanation: The 「の」 in 「この」 has merged into one word with the prefix. Don't read it as noun + の.

meaning: Words that point to places: “here”, “there”, “over there” and “where”.
connection: Used alone, as subject or predicate, or with particles (ここは／そこに／どこへ, etc.)

senses.label: ここ: here
senses.meaning: Points to where the speaker is, or nearby: “here”.
senses.connection: ここ + は／に／で／から, etc.
examples: This is the library.
Please write your name here.

senses.label: そこ: there (near you)
senses.meaning: Points to where the listener is, or nearby. It also refers to a place just mentioned: “there”.
senses.connection: そこ + は／に／で, etc.
examples: The restroom is right there.
There's a bookstore in front of the station. I'll wait for you there.

senses.label: あそこ: over there
senses.meaning: Points to a place far from both speaker and listener: “over there”.
senses.connection: あそこ + は／に／で, etc.
examples: There's a bank over there.
That restaurant over there is cheap.

senses.label: どこ: where
senses.meaning: A question word asking about a place: “where?” Add 「か」 for “somewhere”; use 「も〜ない」 for “nowhere”.
senses.connection: どこ + ですか／に／へ／で, etc.
examples: Where is the station?
Where are you going for summer vacation?

notes: The polite forms are 「こちら・そちら・あちら・どちら」. They are common in shops and offices.
To ask about someone's company, school or country, 「どちら」 is more polite: 「お国はどちらですか」.
At the start of a sentence, 「そこで」 can also be a conjunction meaning “so, then”.

daily.title: Asking the way
daily.description: A tourist asks a passerby where the station is.
daily.example: Excuse me, where is the station?

daily.title: Meeting a friend
daily.description: On the phone, telling a friend where you are.
daily.example: I'm in front of the bookstore now. Come over here.

daily.title: Giving directions
daily.description: Pointing far away to show where the convenience store is.
daily.example: The convenience store is over there.

work.title: Showing a new coworker around
work.description: Pointing to the copier across the office.
work.example: The copy machine is over there.

work.title: Showing someone their desk
work.description: Telling a new coworker where they sit.
work.example: Your desk is right there, Tanaka-san.

etymology: Part of the ko-so-a-do system. 「〜こ」 is the ending for places: 「こ＋こ」, 「そ＋こ」, 「ど＋こ」. The far form is not 「あこ」 but 「あそこ」. It is thought to come from older words like 「かしこ」, so it is an exception.

similar.title: 〜これ・それ・あれ・どれ
similar.explanation: The 「これ」 set points to things; the 「ここ」 set points to places. 「これは何ですか」 asks about a thing; 「ここはどこですか」 asks about a place.

similar.title: 〜この・その・あの・どの
similar.explanation: The 「この」 set describes a noun; the 「ここ」 set stands alone for a place.

similar.title: 〜question word + か
similar.explanation: 「どこか」 means “somewhere”, an indefinite use. 「どこ」 alone asks “where?”.

title: 〜から (starting point)
meaning: Follows a noun to show a starting point in time or place, or the source of an action or information: “from ...”.

senses.label: Starting time
senses.meaning: Shows when an action or state begins: “from ... (o'clock)”. Often paired with 「まで」.
senses.connection: Time noun + から (〜まで)
examples: Class starts at nine.
I work from Monday to Friday.

senses.label: Starting place
senses.meaning: Shows where movement starts: “from (a place)”.
senses.connection: Place noun + から + 来る・出る・帰る, etc.
examples: I came from China.
I walk from the station to my house.

senses.label: Source (person or thing)
senses.meaning: Shows where something or some information comes from: “from (someone)”. Often used with 「もらう」, 「借りる」 and 「聞く」.
senses.connection: Person + から + もらう・借りる・聞く・届く, etc.
examples: I got a letter from my mother.
I heard about that from my teacher.

senses.label: Way in or out
senses.meaning: Shows the opening you pass through: “through (a window, door)”.
senses.connection: 窓・門・入口, etc. + から + 入る・出る
examples: A cat came in through the window.
Please come in through this entrance.

notes: After a noun, it shows a starting point. After a sentence (だから, 寒いから), it shows a reason. That is a different use.
With 「もらう」 and 「借りる」, the giver can take 「に」 or 「から」. When the giver is an organization like a company or school, 「から」 is normal.
Both 「部屋を出る」 and 「部屋から出る」 work. 「から」 stresses the starting point: coming out from inside.

daily.title: Introducing yourself
daily.description: An international student says where they're from.
daily.example: I'm from Shanghai. Nice to meet you.

daily.title: Asking opening hours
daily.description: Asking a clerk at the door what time the shop opens.
daily.example: What time does this shop open?

daily.title: A gift
daily.description: Telling a friend who gave you something.
daily.example: This is a sweater I got from my grandmother.

work.title: Announcing a meeting
work.description: Telling everyone when the meeting starts.
work.example: The meeting will start at 2 p.m.

work.title: Passing on a message
work.description: Reporting to your boss that a client called.
work.example: A call came in from Company A a little while ago.

etymology: 「から」 is generally linked to old 「から（柄）」, which meant “by way of” or “cause”. In old Japanese, 「から」 mainly marked a place passed through. It later came to mark a starting point, and then “because”.

similar.title: 〜まで (end point)
similar.explanation: 「から」 marks the start and 「まで」 the end. They are often used together: 「九時から五時まで」.

similar.title: 〜から (cause / reason)
similar.explanation: Same form, different use. After a noun it marks a starting point (駅から); after a sentence it gives a reason (雨だから, 寒いから).

similar.title: 〜を (route / departure)
similar.explanation: In 「家を出る」, 「を」 marks the place you leave, focusing on the act of leaving. 「家から出る」 focuses on the starting point. Some phrases like 「大学を卒業する」 only take 「を」.

similar.title: 〜から〜まで
similar.explanation: 「から」 and 「まで」 together show the start and end of a range.

meaning: Denies the first part and confirms the second: “not A, but B”. Used to correct or clarify.
connection: Noun + じゃなくて／ではなくて／ではなく + noun (だ)

senses.label: Not A but B (casual)
senses.meaning: First deny A, then give the correct B. Used to correct a misunderstanding or your own words. 「じゃなくて」 is casual.
senses.connection: Noun A + じゃなくて + noun B
examples: This isn't tea, it's coffee.
I'm not a student, I'm a teacher.
It's not today, it's tomorrow.

senses.label: Not A but B (formal)
senses.meaning: 「ではなくて」 and 「ではなく」 are more formal. They are common in writing, the news and formal situations.
senses.connection: Noun A + ではなくて／ではなく + noun B
examples: The meeting is on the fifth floor, not the third.
What matters is not money but health.

senses.label: Correcting an action
senses.meaning: After a verb or a sentence, use 「〜のではなく／〜んじゃなくて」: “not ..., but ...”.
senses.connection: Verb plain form + の (ん) + ではなく／じゃなくて
examples: Don't just memorize it. Understand it.
I'm not angry, I'm worried about you.

notes: 「じゃ」 is the casual contraction of 「では」. Use 「ではなく」 in formal writing.
In 「AではなくB」, B is the correct part. The focus is on what comes second.
「〜だけじゃなくて」 means “not only ... but also ...”. That is a different meaning.
In speech, 「じゃなくて」 can also start a sentence to correct yourself: “No, I mean ...”.

daily.title: Fixing an order
daily.description: The waiter brought the wrong drink, and the customer explains.
daily.example: Excuse me, I ordered it hot, not iced.

daily.title: Explaining your nationality
daily.description: Someone thinks you're Japanese, so you correct them.
daily.example: I'm not Japanese, I'm Chinese.

daily.title: The wrong time
daily.description: A friend got the meeting time wrong, and you correct them.
daily.example: It's not three, it's four.

work.title: Correcting the meeting place
work.description: Telling coworkers the meeting place has changed.
work.example: The meeting will be held at the branch office, not the head office.

work.title: Explaining the approach
work.description: A manager tells the team what matters most.
work.example: What matters is quality, not quantity.

etymology: It comes from 「ではない」, the negative of 「だ」, turned into the te-form 「ではなくて」 to link two parts. In speech 「では」 contracts to 「じゃ」, and in writing the 「て」 is often dropped: 「ではなく」.

similar.title: 〜じゃない・〜ではありません
similar.explanation: 「じゃない」 just says “it's not A” and ends the sentence. 「じゃなくて」 denies A and then goes on to give the correct B.

similar.title: 〜なくて (cause)
similar.explanation: The 「なくて」 in 「わからなくて困った」 gives a cause. 「AじゃなくてB」 is a correction: “not A, but B”.

similar.title: 〜くて・〜で (linking adjectives and nouns)
similar.explanation: 「静かで、きれいだ」 links two positive things. 「AじゃなくてB」 first denies, then confirms.

title: 〜と思う (I think)
meaning: Expresses the speaker's thoughts, opinions or guesses: “I think ...”.
connection: Plain form + と思う (noun / na-adjective + だと思う)

senses.label: Giving an opinion
senses.meaning: States your view or judgment: “I think ...”. 「〜と思います」 sounds softer than a flat statement.
senses.connection: Verb / i-adjective plain form + と思う; noun / na-adjective + だと思う
examples: I think this movie is interesting.
I think Japanese is difficult.
I think he's a good person.

senses.label: Guessing
senses.meaning: Makes a guess about something uncertain: “I think ... will ...”. Often used with 「たぶん」 or 「きっと」.
senses.connection: Plain form + と思う (たぶん・きっと〜と思う)
examples: I think it will rain tomorrow.
I think Tanaka-san probably won't come.

senses.label: Negating or asking opinions
senses.meaning: To deny a view, use 「〜とは思わない」. To ask someone's opinion, use 「〜と思いますか」.
senses.connection: Plain form + とは思わない／と思いますか
examples: I don't believe that story is true.
Do you think these clothes are expensive?

notes: Nouns and na-adjectives need 「だ」: ○「きれいだと思う」, ✕「きれいと思う」.
「〜と思う」 is only for the speaker's own thoughts. For someone else's, use 「〜と思っている」.
Unlike English “I don't think he'll come”, Japanese usually negates the inner part: 「来ないと思う」 is more common than 「来るとは思わない」.
In casual speech, people often say 「〜って思う」.

daily.title: Rating a restaurant
daily.description: After eating with a friend, you share your impression.
daily.example: I think this place is really good.

daily.title: Checking the sky
daily.description: Before going out, you guess the weather to your family.
daily.example: I think it'll rain from the afternoon.

daily.title: Asking a friend
daily.description: Trying on clothes and asking a friend what they think.
daily.example: Do you think this color suits me?

work.title: Speaking at a meeting
work.description: Gently giving your opinion in a meeting.
work.example: I think this plan needs a little more time.

work.title: Estimating progress
work.description: Your boss asks if the work will be done on time.
work.example: I think it will be done by Friday.

etymology: 「思う」 originally meant “to think in one's heart, to long for”. 「と」 is the quoting particle. It puts the thought in front like a quoted sentence.

similar.title: 〜と思っている
similar.explanation: 「〜と思っている」 shows a thought that continues, and can be used for other people: 「彼は日本へ行きたいと思っている」. 「〜と思う」 is mostly the speaker's judgment right now.

similar.title: 〜(よ)うと思う
similar.explanation: With the volitional form (行こう, 食べよう), it shows your own plan: 「明日行こうと思う」. Plain form + と思う shows an opinion or guess.

similar.title: 〜でしょう
similar.explanation: 「でしょう」 is also a guess, but more objective, as in weather forecasts. 「と思う」 sounds like the speaker's personal view.

similar.title: 〜だろうと思う
similar.explanation: Adding 「だろう」 before 「と思う」 makes the guess less certain and softer.

title: 〜と言う (quotation)
meaning: Reports what someone said, or gives a name: “say ...”, “be called ...”.

senses.label: Direct quotation
senses.meaning: Puts someone's exact words in 「」 and reports them as they were: “(someone) said, '...'”.
senses.connection: 「Exact words」 + と言う／と言いました
examples: My mother said, “Go to bed early.”
In Japan, people say “itadakimasu” before eating.

senses.label: Indirect quotation
senses.meaning: Reports the content in the plain form, not the exact words: “(someone) said that ...”.
senses.connection: Plain form + と言う／と言いました (noun / na-adjective + だと言う)
examples: Tanaka-san said he won't come tomorrow.
My friend said this shop is cheap.

senses.label: Names and words
senses.meaning: Gives a name or says what a word is: “be called ...”. To ask what something is called, use 「何と言いますか」.
senses.connection: Name / word + と言います／何と言いますか
examples: My name is Wang.
What is this called in Japanese?
This flower is called sakura.

notes: A direct quote keeps the original style and tense. An indirect quote changes it to the plain form.
To pass on what someone said, 「〜と言っていました」 is common.
In casual speech, people often say 「〜って言う」.
「〜という + noun」 (「田中という人」) means “a ... called ...”. That is a different pattern.

daily.title: Passing on a message
daily.description: Telling a family member what a friend said on the phone.
daily.example: Ken said he can't make it today.

daily.title: Learning words
daily.description: Asking a Japanese friend what something is called in Japanese.
daily.example: What is this called in Japanese?

daily.title: Introducing yourself
daily.description: Saying your name when you meet someone for the first time.
daily.example: Nice to meet you. My name is Lee.

work.title: Reporting to your boss
work.description: Passing on a client's reply from a phone call.
work.example: The manager at Company A said he will reply next week.

work.title: Answering the phone
work.description: Politely asking the caller's name.
work.example: Excuse me, may I have your name?

etymology: 「言う」 originally meant “to put into words”. 「と」 is the quoting particle that marks what was said. 「言う」 is pronounced 「ゆう」 but written 「いう」.

similar.title: 〜という (called / named)
similar.explanation: 「AというB」 comes before a noun: “a B called A” (「田中という人」). 「〜と言う」 is the predicate: “say ...”.

similar.title: 〜と言っていた
similar.explanation: 「〜と言っていた」 is the usual way to pass on what someone else said. It sounds more natural than 「〜と言った」.

similar.title: 〜って (quotation / topic)
similar.explanation: 「って」 is the casual form of 「と（言う）」, as in 「明日休みだって」 (I heard tomorrow's a day off).

similar.title: 〜と思う
similar.explanation: It also quotes with 「と」. 「と言う」 quotes words spoken out loud; 「と思う」 quotes thoughts in your head.

title: 〜は〜より〜 (comparison)
meaning: Uses B as a standard and says A is more so in some way: “A is more ... than B”.
connection: Noun A + は + noun B + より + adjective / verb

senses.label: A is more ... than B
senses.meaning: What comes before 「より」 is the standard, B. The sentence describes the topic, A: “A is ...-er than B”.
senses.connection: AはBより + i-adjective／na-adjective／verb
examples: Tokyo is bigger than Osaka.
Today is colder than yesterday.
My older brother is taller than me.

senses.label: Stronger emphasis
senses.meaning: 「よりも」 is stronger than 「より」 and stresses what you compare with.
senses.connection: AはBよりも + adjective / verb
examples: Health is more important than money.
My younger sister is even better at cooking than I am.

senses.label: Comparing actions
senses.meaning: With verbs, it compares two ways of doing things or their degree: “more ... than ...”.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + より + 〜ほうがいい, etc. / noun + より + verb
examples: The train gets there earlier than the bus.
Rather than watching, I want to try it myself.

notes: What comes before 「より」 is the standard, not the winner. Watch the order: 「AはBより高い」 = A is higher than B.
Japanese adjectives don't change for comparison; there is no “-er” or “more”. Add 「もっと」 or 「ずっと」 when you want emphasis.
To ask which of two is more ..., use 「AとBとどちらが〜」. Answer with 「Bのほうが〜」.
「より」 can also come before an adjective as an adverb (「より良い」 = better). This is written style.

daily.title: Talking about the weather
daily.description: Chatting with your family as you head out in the morning.
daily.example: It's warmer today than yesterday, isn't it?

daily.title: Comparing products
daily.description: Comparing the prices of two items in a shop.
daily.example: This one's cheaper than that one.

daily.title: Talking about family
daily.description: Telling a friend about your younger brother.
daily.example: My younger brother is taller than me.

work.title: Reporting sales
work.description: Telling your boss about this month's sales.
work.example: Sales this month went up compared with last month.

work.title: Comparing plans
work.description: Comparing two plans in a meeting.
work.example: Plan A costs less than Plan B.

etymology: In old Japanese, 「より」 marked a starting point or route (“from”). It later came to mark a standard of comparison (“compared with”). Today 「から」 mostly handles “from”; 「より」 as “from” survives only in writing (「九時より開始」).

similar.title: 〜より〜のほうが
similar.explanation: 「BよりAのほうが〜」 puts the focus on A and is often used to answer “which is more ...?”. 「AはBより〜」 talks about A as the topic.

similar.title: 〜と〜とどちらが
similar.explanation: A question pattern for comparing two things: “Which is more ..., A or B?”

similar.title: 〜ほど〜ない
similar.explanation: 「AはBほど〜ない」 means “A is not as ... as B”, a negative comparison. 「AはBより〜」 is a positive comparison.

similar.title: 〜の中で〜がいちばん
similar.explanation: For three or more, it picks the “most ...” one. 「より」 compares just two.

title: 〜なあ・〜な (exclamation)
meaning: Comes at the end of a sentence to show the speaker's feelings, emotion or wishes. It is usually said to oneself.
connection: Plain form + なあ／な (noun / na-adjective + だなあ)

senses.label: Exclamation
senses.meaning: A natural reaction when you see or feel something: “What a ...!”, “So ...!”
senses.connection: i-adjective + なあ; noun / na-adjective + だなあ
examples: It's so hot today.
What a beautiful view.
This cake is so good.

senses.label: Wishes
senses.meaning: After 「〜たい」, 「〜といい」 or 「ほしい」, it shows a wish: “I wish ...”, “I really want ...”.
senses.connection: 〜たいなあ／〜といいなあ／〜がほしいなあ
examples: I really want to go to the beach this summer.
I wish I had a new computer.

senses.label: Looking back
senses.meaning: Used when remembering the past with feeling. Often follows the past form.
senses.connection: Past form + なあ／な
examples: My school days were so much fun.
That trip was great.

notes: 「なあ」 is mainly said to yourself and doesn't expect a reply. To seek agreement, use 「ね」.
「なあ」 is more emotional than 「な」. Don't use it with older people or in formal settings.
Dictionary form + 「な」 can be a prohibition (「行くな！」 = Don't go!). Don't mix them up.
「〜かなあ」 shows wondering or doubt. That is a different use.

daily.title: Seeing a great view
daily.description: Talking to yourself when you see a beautiful view on a trip.
daily.example: Wow, Mt. Fuji is so beautiful.

daily.title: Monday morning
daily.description: Getting up on Monday and not wanting to go to work.
daily.example: Ugh, I wish I could sleep more.

daily.title: Envying a friend
daily.description: A friend says they're going on a trip, and you're jealous.
daily.example: Hawaii? Lucky you!

work.title: Working late
work.description: Murmuring to yourself after working late into the night.
work.example: What a busy day it was.

work.title: In a novel
work.description: Characters' inner thoughts in novels often use 「なあ」.
work.example: I wish I could go back to that town once more.

etymology: 「な」 is an old sentence-ending particle for exclamation. 「なあ」 is 「な」 stretched out for stronger feeling. It is thought to belong to the same family as the old exclamation particles 「な」 and 「かな」.

similar.title: 〜ね
similar.explanation: 「ね」 is said to the listener to seek agreement (「暑いですね」). 「なあ」 is usually an exclamation to yourself (「暑いなあ」).

similar.title: 〜な (prohibition)
similar.explanation: Dictionary form + 「な」 is a rough prohibition (「触るな」 = Don't touch). Exclamation 「な」 usually follows adjectives, past forms or 「〜たい」.

similar.title: 〜かな
similar.explanation: 「かな」 shows a question or doubt: “I wonder if ...”. 「なあ」 is an exclamation or wish.

title: 〜 (verb plain form) + noun (relative clause)
meaning: Put a verb in the plain form right before a noun to describe it. This works like a relative clause in English: “the book (that) I bought”.
connection: Verb plain form (dictionary form, た-form, ない-form, ている-form) + noun

senses.label: Dictionary form + noun
senses.meaning: Shows a habit, something planned, or a general fact: “the ... (I) do / will do”.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + noun
examples: The coffee I drink every morning is good.
Please tell me the place we're going tomorrow.

senses.label: た-form + noun
senses.meaning: Shows a finished action: “the ... (I) did”.
senses.connection: Verb た-form + noun
examples: This is the book I bought yesterday.
The movie I saw last week was interesting.

senses.label: ない-form + noun
senses.meaning: Shows a negative: “the ... (I) don't / didn't do”.
senses.connection: Verb ない-form + noun
examples: I look up words I don't know in a dictionary.
Some people don't eat meat.

senses.label: ている-form + noun
senses.meaning: Shows an action in progress or an ongoing state. Often used to describe what people are wearing or doing.
senses.connection: Verb ている-form + noun
examples: Who is the person wearing glasses?
The person reading a book over there is my older brother.

senses.label: With a subject
senses.meaning: The subject inside the clause takes 「が」 (or 「の」), not 「は」.
senses.connection: Noun + が + verb plain form + noun
examples: The food my mother makes is delicious.
The town I live in is quiet.

notes: Use the plain form before a noun, not the ます-form: ✕「昨日買いました本」.
The subject inside the clause takes 「が」 or 「の」, not 「は」: ○「私が買った本」, ✕「私は買った本」.
Japanese has no relative pronouns like “who”, “which” or “that”. The whole clause simply goes in front of the noun.
Adjectives can describe nouns directly, too: i-adjectives as they are, na-adjectives with 「な」, and nouns with 「の」.

daily.title: Introducing a friend
daily.description: Showing your family who is in a photo.
daily.example: The person smiling in this photo is my friend.

daily.title: Looking for something
daily.description: Asking your family where something is.
daily.example: Where's the bread I bought yesterday?

daily.title: Recommending a book
daily.description: Recommending a book you've read to a friend.
daily.example: This is a book by my favorite author.

work.title: Checking materials
work.description: Asking a coworker about the documents you'll use.
work.example: Have you prepared the materials we'll use in the meeting?

work.title: Explaining the situation
work.description: Telling your boss about unfinished work.
work.example: There are three tasks that aren't finished yet.

etymology: Japanese verbs and adjectives have an “attributive form” that goes directly before a noun. In modern Japanese, a verb's attributive form is the same as its dictionary form, so the plain form can describe a noun directly.

similar.title: 〜の (replacing が in a relative clause)
similar.explanation: Inside the clause, the subject 「が」 can become 「の」: 「母が作った料理」 = 「母の作った料理」.

similar.title: 〜な + noun
similar.explanation: Na-adjectives need 「な」 before a noun (静かな町). A verb in the plain form goes straight before the noun with nothing added.

similar.title: 〜 (plain-form clause) + noun (noun modification)
similar.explanation: A broader topic that includes adjective and noun sentences describing nouns. This entry focuses on the different verb forms.

title: 〜 (number) + counter (〜本・〜人・〜枚など)
meaning: When counting in Japanese, you add a counter after the number that shows the type of thing, a bit like “two sheets of paper” or “three bottles of water” in English.
connection: Number + counter (〜つ・〜本・〜人・〜枚, etc.)

senses.label: 〜つ: general
senses.meaning: Works for most objects and abstract things. It only goes up to ten (「とお」); from eleven on, use plain numbers.
senses.connection: ひとつ・ふたつ・みっつ…とお／いくつ
examples: Three apples, please.
I have one question.
How many eggs do you need?

senses.label: 〜人: people
senses.meaning: Counts people. 「一人」 is 「ひとり」, 「二人」 is 「ふたり」, and from three on it's 「〜にん」.
senses.connection: 一人（ひとり）・二人（ふたり）・三人（さんにん）…／何人
examples: There are four people in my family.
There are twenty students in the classroom.

senses.label: 〜本: long, thin things
senses.meaning: Counts long, thin things like pens, bottles, umbrellas and trees. Also used for movies and phone calls. The sound changes: いっぽん, にほん, さんぼん.
senses.connection: 一本（いっぽん）・二本（にほん）・三本（さんぼん）…／何本
examples: I bought two pens.
Three bottles of beer, please.

senses.label: 〜枚: thin, flat things
senses.meaning: Counts thin, flat things like paper, plates, shirts, stamps and tickets.
senses.connection: 一枚・二枚・三枚…／何枚
examples: Five stamps, please.
I have two T-shirts.

senses.label: Other common counters
senses.meaning: 「〜冊」 for books, 「〜台」 for machines and cars, 「〜匹」 for small animals, 「〜杯」 for cups and bowls of food or drink, and 「〜個」 for small objects.
senses.connection: Number + 冊・台・匹・杯・個, etc.
examples: I borrowed three books.
We have two cats at home.
I drank a cup of coffee.

notes: The number + counter usually goes right before the verb with no particle: 「りんごを三つ買う」. You can also say 「三つのりんご」.
The number often changes its sound before a counter, as in 「一本（いっぽん）」, 「三杯（さんばい）」 and 「六匹（ろっぴき）」.
To ask how many, use 「何 + counter」 (何本, 何枚) or 「いくつ」.
「一人で」 means “alone, by oneself”, as in 「一人で行きます」.

daily.title: At a restaurant
daily.description: Telling the staff how many people are in your group.
daily.example: Hi, there are three of us.

daily.title: At a convenience store
daily.description: Telling the clerk how many bottles of water you want.
daily.example: Two bottles of water, please.

daily.title: At the post office
daily.description: Buying stamps.
daily.example: Ten 84-yen stamps, please.

work.title: Preparing for a meeting
work.description: Asking a coworker to copy the meeting materials.
work.example: Please make ten copies of this document.

work.title: Checking stock
work.description: Checking how many machines are left in the storeroom.
work.example: How many computers do we have left?

etymology: 「助数詞」 means “words that help numbers”. Many counters, such as 「本」, 「枚」, 「冊」 and 「台」, came from Chinese and use on-yomi. 「〜つ」 and 「ひとり・ふたり」 are native Japanese ways of counting.

similar.title: 〜目 (ordinal)
similar.explanation: Add 「目」 after a counter to show order: 「三本目」 = the third bottle, 「二人目」 = the second person.

similar.title: 〜ずつ
similar.explanation: Number + counter + 「ずつ」 means “... each”: 「一人二つずつ」 = two for each person.

similar.title: 〜くらい・〜ぐらい
similar.explanation: Number + counter + 「くらい」 means “about”: 「十人ぐらい」 = about ten people.

similar.title: 〜も (emphasizing amount)
similar.explanation: Number + counter + 「も」 stresses a large amount: 「ビールを五本も飲んだ」 = I drank as many as five bottles of beer.

title: 〜しかし (at the start: however)
meaning: Starts a sentence and shows that it goes against or contrasts with the one before: “but”, “however”. Mostly written.

senses.label: Contrast (written)
senses.meaning: Links two sentences when the second goes against what you'd expect: “but, however”. It sounds stiffer than 「でも」 and is common in writing, speeches and the news.
senses.connection: Sentence. + しかし、sentence.
examples: This shop is cheap. However, the food isn't very good.
I studied very hard. However, I failed the exam.

senses.label: Raising a point
senses.meaning: First accept what was said, then give a different view or a problem. Common in essays and meetings.
senses.connection: Sentence. + しかし、problem / different opinion.
examples: The new plan is a good idea. However, it will cost money.

senses.label: Exclamation (spoken)
senses.meaning: At the start of a sentence, it can add feeling, like “Boy, ...” or “Well, ...”. Mostly used by older men.
senses.connection: しかし、+ exclamation
examples: Boy, it sure is hot today.

notes: 「しかし」 is mostly used in writing and formal speech. In daily conversation, people usually say 「でも」 or 「けど」.
It goes at the start of a sentence, usually followed by 「、」. Unlike 「が」 or 「けど」, it can't join two clauses in the middle of one sentence.
A more formal version is 「しかしながら」, common in official documents and the news.

daily.title: Reading the news
daily.description: A news report uses 「しかし」 to link two contrasting facts.
daily.example: The economy is recovering. However, wages haven't risen much.

daily.title: Writing a diary
daily.description: Writing about how the day turned out differently than expected.
daily.example: It was sunny in the morning. However, it started raining in the afternoon.

work.title: Raising an issue in a meeting
work.description: First praising a proposal, then pointing out a problem.
work.example: This plan is interesting. However, I don't think we have enough time.

work.title: Writing a report
work.description: Explaining a result that went against expectations.
work.example: Sales went up. However, profits went down.

etymology: 「しかし」 is a shortening of old 「しかしながら」 (然しながら). 「しか」 (然) means “so, like that”, so it originally meant “even though it is so”. It can be written 「然し」 or 「併し」, but kana is normal today.

similar.title: 〜でも (at the start: but)
similar.explanation: 「でも」 is casual and common in everyday conversation. 「しかし」 is written and stiff.

similar.title: 〜が (but)
similar.explanation: 「が」 joins two parts in the middle of a sentence (「安いが、まずい」). 「しかし」 starts a new sentence.

similar.title: 〜けど・〜けれども
similar.explanation: 「けど」 joins clauses within a sentence and is common in speech. 「しかし」 is a stand-alone conjunction at the start of a sentence and sounds written.
